events.text:
— Hypothetically, if the U.S. wanted to carry out a naval landing in Iran, they would do it somewhere outside the Persian Gulf, most likely Chabahar or somewhere else in the flat open coasts of Sistan-Balochistan Province.
That way, they don’t need to risk their ships entering the Persian Gulf under heavy anti-ship fire and incoming drones while trying to land their soldiers on a rugged coastline full of fortified positions and artillery emplacements.
In Chabahar, they could bring their ships close enough to the shore with relative safety, under heavy air cover. U.S. jets, drones, and attack helicopters would suppress any anti-ship batteries heavily, and create sufficiently safe conditions for the initial ‘landing’. One also cannot rule out the possibility of deploying U.S. airborne forces to secure key sites before an amphibious landing is attempted.
This might be coupled with increased Balochi terrorist activity across the Iranian rear lines, complicating logistics and the transfer of equipment / reinforcements towards the front. During this phase of the assault, I don’t expect much effective Iranian resistance, due to the overwhelming U.S. firepower (armored vehicles, air support, superior weaponry, etc.)
In Sistan-Balochistan, Iranian ballistic missile platforms, MLRS systems, and armored formations capable of confronting the invading force are also fairly limited in quantity. The initial phase of resistance would thus focus mainly on assymetric warfare; small squads of Iranian ATGM crews, FPV drone operators, IEDs, drones, and what little precision-guided artillery & air support (UAVs) could be scrambled.
This would probably cause enough mayhem on the U.S. side to slow their advance, but it won’t be enough to stop them from making decent progress towards strategic objectives.
However, in my assessment, time will tell a different story. The longer the American force remains on the Iranian shores, the harsher their conditions will deteriorate. The Iranians will reorganize, MANPAD squads and remaining SHORAD systems will likely form too much of a risk for U.S. aviation to provide effective long-term air cover, local civilians would resist occupation with guerilla tactics, and Iran would have moved sufficient amounts of MLRS, missile, and artillery systems to the area to make any sustained American presence a nightmare. It would turn into a full-scale ground war, with Iranian tanks being deployed in combat for the first time since 1988.
I believe the U.S. is currently not willing to tolerate the sheer amounts of losses such an operation would entail. The public is already very opposed to the war, and this opposition would only increase. Dozens if not hundreds of American soldiers would die within the first month of such an operation, possibly thousands after several months. And what’s the strategic goal here? What purpose does it serve? 
The answer is: None. A limited amphibious landing would not bring any benefit to the United States, unless they go all-out. That would entail deploying tens of thousands of troops and securing the entire southern coastline towards the Strait of Hormuz, in an effort to stop the disruption of shipping & bring Iran back to the table.
Realistically? Impossible. The disasters such an operation would bring to the region are unimaginable, and senior U.S. military officials will *hopefully* realize it is a non-starter before they ever embark on this campaign.
Iran would treat such a scenario as total war. A divine Jihad, magnitudes greater than the 8-year long Iran-Iraq war. All red lines would have been finally crossed. And in such a case, the IRGC Aerospace Force will take the entire region down with it. All economic, military and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf will cease to exist. Millions would be mobilized, and it will be a bloodbath on both sides.

The commander of Hamas's Northern Gaza Brigade, who was killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City earlier this week, had been responsible for holding numerous hostages in captivity, the military says.
The IDF says that "following extensive intelligence research," it can reveal that Izz al-Din al-Bik, who was killed on Tuesday, "commanded the captivity of Israeli hostages during the war."
The hostages under Bik's responsibility included Mia Schem, Hisham al-Sayed, Amit Buskila, Uriel Baruch, Corporal Nik Beizer, Sergeant Ron Sherman, Elia Toledano, Shani Louk, Michel Nisenbaum, Staff Sergeant Tamir Nimrodi, Yitzhak Gelerenter, Eitan Levy, Hanan Yablonka, Ron Benjamin, and Orion Hernandez.
Bik had been in the role since the previous Northern Gaza Brigade commander, Ahmed Ghandour, was killed by Israel on November 10, 2023, according to the military and Hamas.
Before that, he held other top roles, including chief of intelligence in the Northern Gaza Brigade and commander of the Western Jabalia Battalion.
"In these roles, he advanced and financed numerous attacks against Israeli civilians and was among the founders of Hamas’s Nukhba forces in northern Gaza," the military says.
In addition, Bik "commanded and participated in the infiltration into Israeli territory" during the October 7, 2023, onslaught, according to the IDF.

🇾🇪🇸🇦 Yemen’s Houthis hold leverage as Saudi Arabia faces talks on their terms
Ansar Allah’s[ coastal advances](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74670) and ability to carry out long-range strikes allow the movement to enter any future negotiations with Saudi Arabia from a stronger position, notes The Cradle.
The Gulf kingdom’s military gamble has made the path back to talks more complicated.
 
♦️ the Houthis have seized control of swathes of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and key strategic locations in and[ around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74821), including[ the key port city of Mokha ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74540)
♦️cross-border strikes have brought the conflict back into Saudi territory, while attacks and[ threats affecting Red Sea shipping ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75123)have added pressure on the kingdom’s economic interests
♦️ UAE’s withdrawal left Saudi Arabia managing fragmented local allies (STC, Giants Brigades and Tariq Saleh-linked forces) mired in internal rivalry
♦️ earlier diplomatic track remains unfinished: 2023 UN-led peace roadmap envisioned renewed oil exports, reopened roads, payment of public sector salaries, eased restrictions on Sanaa Airport and Hodeidah Port, but key commitments were never fully implemented
Saudi Arabia’s failed attempt to reorganize its proxies and seek outside[ support from the US](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74908) or via the [Mecca defense pact ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75480)has not restored the initiative. 
By contrast, the Houthis enter any future discussion from a position of consolidated territorial gains and proven ability to enforce their demands. 
Officials in Sanaa stress that past delays and unfulfilled commitments make superficial ceasefires insufficient, and concrete steps like ending the blockade, releasing prisoners, withdrawing occupying forces, and providing monitored compensation must come first.

🇾🇪💥 Ansar Allah launches Taiz offensive to cut Saudi-backed forces’ supply lines
The Houthis have entered southern Taiz, taking control of parts of the city and expanding their gains in southwestern Yemen, Tasnim News reports.
Videos circulating on X also appear to show Saudi-backed militias fleeing Houthi advances, while others feature Ansar Allah units deployed near the outskirts of Taiz calling on adversaries to surrender over loudspeakers: “You are under siege. O sons of Mohammed bin Salman, O sons of Netanyahu, surrender!”
The city of Taiz is of utmost importance to the Houthis, as control of it would allow them to cut the main supply lines of pro-Saudi forces and open a direct route south toward Aden.
👉 On October 1, the Houthis have taken control of the road linking Sanaa and Taiz, according to Tasnim’s correspondent in Yemen.
A large section of the strategic Taiz-Aden route, which links the city to its southern and western countryside and extends toward Lahij Governorate, has also allegedly fallen into Houthi hands, according to OSINT accounts on X.
The Houthis have launched operations at multiple points across Taiz province and city since September 30, with clashes reported in eastern Taiz and Al-Turbah, the administrative center of Ash Shamayatayn district in southern Taiz province.
Earlier this week, Arab News reported a “massive” buildup of tanks, missiles, and other weaponry by Ansar Allah, which it described as preparations for a possible offensive on Taiz, citing pro-Saudi military sources on the ground.

🇾🇪🗣 Houthi strikes expose cracks in Saudi Arabia’s Mecca defense pact
The[ joint defense pact ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74677)signed in Mecca by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey in August on paper committed the three countries to treating an attack on one as an attack on all.
When[ Saudi Arabia’s military gambit](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73159) triggered retaliatory missile and drone strikes by Yemen’s Ansar Allah just weeks after the pact was signed, targeting Saudi infrastructure and military sites, the kingdom found itself essentially fending off the attacks alone, say analysts.
Saudi Arabia turned to the US rather than its Mecca pact partners - only for Donald Trump to initially reject its request for help against Ansar Allah. The US president later reversed course, but then reportedly pulled back from [planned strikes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74908) at the eleventh hour.
🔍The Mecca pact produced plenty of diplomatic backing: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey condemned the Houthi strikes, and their military chiefs discussed intelligence sharing, military coordination and integrating capabilities.
But the much-touted defense pact offered the Gulf state no immediate military intervention, assess regional experts.

Kushner brokers Gaza diplomacy while his firm profits from Israeli investor tied to arms makers — reports
Jared Kushner has played a major role in Trump’s Gaza diplomacy while his private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, remains the largest shareholder in Israel’s [Phoenix Financial](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/57782), CNN reported.
Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in Elbit Systems and at least eight other companies supplying Israel’s military with drones, warships, tank components, artillery fuzes and demolition equipment. Affinity does not directly own those defense stocks, but it benefits when Phoenix profits. Pasted text
Kushner’s firm sold a quarter of its Phoenix stake in July for more than $340 million, a return exceeding five times its initial purchase, while retaining a 7.4% stake worth over $1 billion.
Kushner operates as an unpaid envoy, meaning he is not subject to the financial disclosure rules that would apply to a formal government official. CNN found no evidence that his diplomatic decisions directly influenced the investments. His lawyer also denied Kushner had any role in Phoenix’s investment choices.
Yet Kushner himself has said:
“What people call conflicts of interests, Steve and I call experience and trusted relationships.”
CNN also found Phoenix stakes in companies whose business benefited from Israel’s wars, including Elbit Systems, whose stock rose more than 165% after the Gaza war began. Pasted text
